     "subtitle": "From Economics to the Delivery Room: How Personal Trauma Shaped the Life Calling of Andrea Piškor",
     "screenshot_description": "Andrea Piškor explains the importance of a dignified birth experience and recognizing motherhood as a joyful event.",
     "content": "With opening words, Željka Markić opens a conversation on topics that cut into the most intimate, yet socially exceptionally important pores of family life – pregnancy, childbirth, and early motherhood. As a guest, she introduces **Andrea Piškor**, a master of economics, former teacher, and mother of three boys and one girl, who today runs her own business for education and support for pregnant women, mothers, and fathers.\n\nAndrea Piškor describes how her professional turning point was prompted by her own experience of her first birth fifteen years ago. Although she prepared by reading literature such as *A Spiritual Approach to Childbirth*, she faced a prolonged, medically complex birth in an overburdened hospital system. A devastating moment was the feeling of physical and emotional woundedness, additionally intensified by the common social saying: *“All is well as long as you and the baby are alive”*. For the guest, that phrase represented a kind of “slap in the face” that disregards the dignity of the woman.\n\nThrough spiritual maturation and growth in faith, Andrea Piškor recognized that God's plan for motherhood is neither trauma nor humiliation, but joy. The scientifically established onset of labor is marked by the secretion of **oxytocin** – the hormone of love and safety – which confirms that childbirth in its essence ought to be a safe and supportive process. After the birth of her third child, she made the decision to completely leave her previous profession and dedicate herself to the vocation of childbirth educator and birth companion.",

     "subtitle": "Comprehensive Preparation and the Role of the Companion: More Than Technical Information",
     "screenshot_description": "Andrea Piškor explains the structure of her educational program and the role of the continuous companion.",
     "content": "Speaking about her work with couples, Andrea Piškor emphasizes that she combines the role of childbirth educator and continuous companion. Her program encompasses four key segments: preparation for pregnancy, childbirth, postpartum, and breastfeeding. Although we live in an information age, the guest warns of the paradox of profound misinformation – many couples do not know even the basic anatomical and physiological processes of their own bodies, such as the structure of the uterus or the mechanism of conception.\n\nEducation provides a foundation on the basis of which parents can make decisions in peace. She emphasizes that there is no universally “good” or “bad” decision, but rather the correct one is that which the partners make together and in an informed manner. Childbirth is an unpredictable process and cannot be planned entirely, but knowing the stages of giving birth brings much-needed inner stability.\n\nAs a companion, Andrea Piškor remains available to parents during pregnancy, the very onset of labor contractions, and in the first weeks after childbirth. In doing so, she clearly sets the boundaries of her role: she does not make decisions instead of the parents, does not negotiate with hospital staff on their behalf, but acts as firm emotional and practical support that empowers the mother and father.",

     "subtitle": "Continuous Accompaniment of the Pregnant Woman: Resolving Deep Fears and Respecting Maternal Intuition",
     "screenshot_description": "Željka Markić and Andrea Piškor discuss the importance of trust and resolving fears before childbirth.",
     "content": "In the continuation of the conversation, the importance of timely connection between the pregnant woman and the educator is emphasized, ideally already around the middle of pregnancy. Through months of continuity, deep mutual trust is built, which enables opening up sensitive topics that transcend the technical phases of childbirth. Andrea Piškor notes that many women, even when expecting their fifth or sixth child, cope with deeply rooted fear due to earlier traumatic experiences or the lack of understanding from their environment toward openness to life.\n\nFrom her own medical and parental experience, Željka Markić supports the thesis on the necessity of respecting **maternal intuition**. Decisions about the moment of departure for the maternity hospital or the way of coping with contractions should stem from the feelings of the woman herself and her agreement with her husband, and not from imposed expectations of others.\n\nChildbirth is not exclusively a medical procedure, the guest warns, although the domestic healthcare system often treats it as such. A woman is an integral being – of spirit, soul, and body. If the laboring woman is not in a safe and supportive environment, stress and fear block the natural secretion of oxytocin, which directly complicates and slows down the entire physiological course of giving birth.",

     "subtitle": "Childbirth Is a Marathon, Not a Sprint: Challenges in Maternity Wards and Comparison with Foreign Practices",
     "screenshot_description": "Andrea Piškor speaks about the overburdening of midwives and the advantages of an individualized approach abroad.",
     "content": "As one of the greatest obstacles to a positive birth experience, Andrea Piškor cites modern impatience and culturally imposed pressure that childbirth must end quickly. She compares birth to a marathon that requires its time, peace, and composure. The early period of mild contractions spent in the warmth of home, along with the family's preparation for the arrival of a new member, can strengthen the married couple and bring spiritual growth instead of trauma.\n\nOn the other hand, the care system in domestic maternity hospitals faces a chronic shortage of medical staff. Midwives often run throughout the entire shift caring for too large a number of laboring women, which is why they objectively have no time to dedicate to the psychological state of an individual woman. Due to overburdened capacities, situations of redirecting pregnant women to other maternity hospitals have also occurred, which creates immense stress.\n\nComparing domestic conditions with Western systems, the interlocutors cite examples in which a pregnant woman collaborates from the beginning of pregnancy with a specific midwife who visits her at home and accompanies her at birth. Also, they highlight the practice of timely consultations with anesthesiologists where the pros and cons of epidural analgesia are discussed in peace, which in the long run saves the healthcare system both time and money.",

     "subtitle": "The Role and Empowerment of Fathers: Key Support in the Delivery Room and the Power of Informed Consent",
     "screenshot_description": "Andrea Piškor explains why the husband and father of the child takes precedence over a companion in the delivery room.",
     "content": "Speaking of presence in the delivery room, Andrea Piškor emphasizes that she always gives precedence to the fathers of the child over external companions. During education, she strives to relieve men of the false belief that they must perform complicated procedures at birth. Their fundamental and most valuable role is a calm, steady presence and providing a sense of security to their own wife. Witnessing the birth of a child together raises marriage and the family to a completely new level of connection.\n\nTouching upon the topic of the **birth plan**, the interlocutors explain that it does not have to be a rigid administrative document, but rather a starting point for a conversation within the couple about their wishes and possibilities within the maternity hospital. A key element of a positive experience is **informed consent**.\n\nMedical interventions, such as the rupturing of membranes or episiotomy, are not enemies in themselves – they save lives when medically indicated. However, the problem arises when interventions are performed routinely, without the knowledge and consent of the laboring woman. Andrea Piškor concludes that a woman will not experience trauma due to the medical intervention itself if the physician previously explained the reasons to her and enabled her to participate actively in making the decision.",

     "content": "In the continuation of the conversation, Željka Markić and Andrea Piškor touch upon the topic of medical interventions, with special emphasis on episiotomy. Markić observes that France records an exceptionally low rate of performing episiotomy of around 8 percent, while in countries like Croatia, Germany, and Austria that percentage is around 20 percent. The host points out that French professional guidelines were adopted on the basis of research that proved that episiotomy does not prevent more severe consequences to the extent that was previously assumed.\n\nAndrea Piškor emphasizes that numerous modern studies show the absence of real benefit from routine episiotomy. Nevertheless, the key problem in the domestic system lies in the inconsistency of practices; the application of interventions often does not depend on general protocols, but on the individual physician who is on duty at that moment. Željka Markić adds that gynecology and obstetrics are among the most stressful branches of medicine because the physician assumes responsibility for a healthy laboring woman and her child, whereby every unforeseen complication creates enormous pressure.\n\nPiškor notes that the head of the delivery room must possess exceptional management skills in order to coordinate shifts and react to the unpredictable number of laboring women who arrive. Due to the overburdening of midwives and physicians, the system often lacks the capacity to dedicate itself to the emotional state of the woman. That is precisely why she emphasizes the necessity of cooperation between medical staff and companions. A positive birth experience in which a woman feels respected is crucial for the postpartum period, because it is proven to reduce the risk of postpartum depression and speed up psychophysical recovery.",

Although medical staff in principle know these advantages, in practice laboring women are still often directed into a lying position.\n\nŽeljka Markić cites the example of the existence of warm water tubs in certain hospitals, which significantly ease enduring contractions and reduce the need for interventions, but are rarely offered to women due to a lack of time and staff to monitor them.      "content": "Moving to the topic of early motherhood, Andrea Piškor points out that breastfeeding is a natural process, but also a skill that is learned and perfected. Because of this, it is easy to believe in myths about how mother's milk is “not strong enough” or how the body cannot produce a sufficient amount of food.\n\nAs a master of economics, Piškor vividly explains that lactation rests on the fundamental economic law of supply and demand: the breast produces as much milk as the baby demands and stimulates by sucking.
